title: From the Text to the Sermon
subtitle: A working method for preparing a sermon that honors the text and lands on a Tuesday afternoon

sections.title: The Relentless Clock
sections.body:
Sunday comes whether you are ready or not. It is the one deadline that cannot move, the one meeting that will be held with or without your preparation, and by Thursday afternoon the panic is familiar. The week got eaten by the hospital, the meeting, the crisis, and the text in front of you is still silent.

Every preacher knows this fear. The fear of standing up with nothing to say.

The answer is not more talent. The answer is a method, a craft you can repeat under pressure when inspiration has not arrived and the clock will not stop. Most bad preaching is not a failure of gifting. It is a failure of process, a sermon thrown together on Saturday night and then defended as Spirit-led. The Spirit is not opposed to your discipline. The Spirit blesses the man who sat in the text on Monday far more reliably than the man who panicked on Saturday. I have preached from panic and I have preached from preparation, and the congregation could always tell the difference even when they could not name it.

sections.title: First, Live in the Text
sections.body:
Begin Monday, not Saturday. Open the passage and read it until it stops being strange and starts being familiar, and then read it past familiar until it becomes strange again, because the second strangeness is where the sermon hides.

Do not reach for commentaries yet. Sit with the text alone first. The text deserves your own wrestling before you borrow anyone else's.

Read it in more than one translation. Read it out loud, because the ear catches what the eye skims. Write down your questions, every one, even the dumb ones, because your questions are your congregation's questions and the passage you find confusing is the passage they find confusing too. Look for what the author is actually doing, not just what the words say but the move the writer is making, the argument, the turn, the weight. Find the one thing the passage is mainly about. Not seven things. One. A sermon that is about everything is about nothing, and the discipline of finding the single beating heart of the text is most of the work. Only after you have wrestled, after you have your own questions and your own read, do you open the commentaries, and then you open the good ones, to check your work and correct your errors and deepen what you found. The commentary is a teacher, not a substitute for thought.

sections.title: From the Text to the Point
sections.body:
Now turn the corner from study to sermon, and this corner is where most preaching dies. You have done the exegesis. You have a heap of true observations. A heap of true observations is not a sermon.

A sermon has one point, sharp enough to remember and large enough to matter. Find it.

Say it in a single sentence, plainly, the kind of sentence a tired person could repeat to a friend on Monday. If you cannot say it in one sentence, you do not yet know what you are preaching, and you will stand up Sunday and wander, and the congregation will wander with you and arrive nowhere. This sentence is the spine. Every part of the sermon either serves it or gets cut, no matter how clever, no matter how much you love it. The deadliest words in a study are but this is so interesting. Interesting is not the standard. Faithful to the text and useful to the people, that is the standard. Then build the bones around the spine. Where are you taking them, how does the text get them there, what is the one move the sermon makes from where they sit now to where the text wants them to stand. Keep it simple enough to follow in real time, because they get one pass at it, with no rewind, with kids squirming and worries pulling at them. Clarity is not a lesser virtue than depth. Clarity is how depth reaches anybody.

sections.title: Make It Land on a Tuesday
sections.body:
A sermon that is true and does not touch the actual lives of the people is a lecture, and they have enough lectures. The question that turns a study into a sermon is brutally simple. So what, on Tuesday.

Not Sunday application that evaporates by lunch. Tuesday application, when the marriage is cold and the boss is cruel and the prayer feels like talking to the ceiling.

Picture the actual people. The man three rows back who lost his job Thursday. The teenager who is not sure any of this is real. The widow in the second pew on her first Sunday alone. Preach the text into their week, not into the abstract. Do not settle for try harder or be nicer, which is law without gospel and crushes people who are already crushed. Show them what this text means for the God who meets them in the specific places their lives are breaking. Get concrete. Vague application changes no one. The sermon that says be more loving changes nobody, and the sermon that says here is what love looks like when your father will not speak to you can change a life. Land it where they live, or do not bother to climb into the pulpit.

sections.title: The Final Hours and the Letting Go
sections.body:
By the end of the week the sermon should be built, and now the work is to make it preachable and then to hand it over. Write it down, or write a full outline, in whatever form lets you preach freely rather than read stiffly. Then cut. Almost every sermon is too long, and the second half of preparation is mostly deleting the things you were proud of.

Preach it out loud before Sunday, to the empty room, because a sermon that lives only on paper has not yet become speech.

Get to Saturday with the work done so Saturday night can be prayer instead of panic. Then, when you have done everything craft can do, let it go. Pray over it and surrender it, because the sermon does not save anyone and you do not save anyone, and the same Spirit who inspired the text is the one who carries it into hearts you cannot reach. Your job was to be faithful to the text and useful to the people and out of the way of the Word. You did the work. Now stop gripping it. Climb into the pulpit, open the Book, and trust the God who has never once needed your eloquence to do what only he can do.
